expectedText:
WRONGFUL FORECLOSURE AND THE VOID-ASSIGNMENT STANDING RULE
Prepared for Jordan Lee · 123 Main St., Woodland Hills, CA 91367

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — INFORMATIONAL ONLY
This sheet states what California law provides on one narrow question that can arise after a nonjudicial foreclosure sale: whether a borrower who was not a party to an assignment of the note and deed of trust may base an action for wrongful foreclosure on the contention that the assignment was void. It is prepared with reference to Jordan Lee, the property at 123 Main St., Woodland Hills, CA 91367, the trustee's sale said to have taken place on or about September 14, 2026, and the foreclosing entity identified as Western Progressive, LLC, as trustee. The clauses that follow reproduce the governing statutory text and the holdings of the California courts that have construed it, together with the questions those courts expressly declined to decide. Nothing here evaluates any document in the chain of title to 123 Main St., Woodland Hills, CA 91367, states whether any cause of action exists, or predicts how a court would rule. This is an information sheet, not legal advice, and it creates no attorney-client relationship.

THE SINGLE QUESTION THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT AGREED TO DECIDE
In Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp. (2016) 62 Cal.4th 919, the California Supreme Court granted review on one question only, and it recited the terms of that limited grant in the opinion. The Court framed the issue as whether a borrower on a home loan secured by a deed of trust may base an action for wrongful foreclosure on allegations that a purported assignment of the note and deed of trust to the foreclosing party bore defects rendering the assignment void. The scope of that grant governs how the rest of the opinion reads: the Court repeatedly identified adjacent questions as outside the limited grant and declined to reach them. Several of the clauses that follow record those declinations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "In an action for wrongful foreclosure on a deed of trust securing a home loan, does the borrower have standing to challenge an assignment of the note and deed of trust on the basis of defects allegedly rendering the assignment void?"
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 926 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  Known gap: The quote is the text of the order limiting review as the opinion reproduces it. It was verified against two independent publishers of the same opinion: the Judicial Council of California's official slip opinion PDF for docket S218973 on courts.ca.gov (extracted twice, with pdfminer.six and with pypdf, which agreed on all body prose and differed only in how they interleaved the caption block and the marginal line numbers), and the Official Reports text as republished by CourtListener. Those two publications are not identical throughout. In the opinion's opening paragraph the slip PDF begins the same question with a lowercase "whether" while the Official Reports text begins it with a capital "Whether"; the quote given here is drawn from the later passage reciting the order itself, where the two publications agree character for character. Quotes were normalized only for benign extraction artifacts before comparison: non-breaking spaces, line-wrap hyphenation, ligatures, and the curly quotation marks and dashes that the two sources encode differently (the courts.ca.gov slip PDF renders opening and closing double quotation marks through a font mapping that extracts as U+2015 and U+2016, and em dashes extract as a double hyphen). No word, number or punctuation mark was changed. The pin cite was read off the star pagination in the CourtListener text, not from memory.

WHAT THE COURT HELD: A VOID ASSIGNMENT, NOT A MERELY VOIDABLE ONE
The Court held that because in a nonjudicial foreclosure only the original beneficiary of a deed of trust, its assignee, or an agent of one of these may direct the trustee to sell the property, an allegation that an assignment in that chain was void rather than merely voidable will support an action for wrongful foreclosure. The Court restated the same holding in its concluding paragraph, describing the consequence of a void assignment as depriving the foreclosing party of any legitimate authority to order a trustee's sale. The distinction the holding turns on — void versus voidable — is set out in a separate clause of this sheet. Whether any assignment affecting 123 Main St., Woodland Hills, CA 91367 falls on either side of that line is not addressed here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "because in a nonjudicial foreclosure only the original beneficiary of a deed of trust or its assignee or agent may direct the trustee to sell the property, an allegation that the assignment was void, and not merely voidable at the behest of the parties to the assignment, will support an action for wrongful foreclosure"
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 923 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "party purportedly took a beneficial interest in the deed of trust was not merely voidable but void, depriving the foreclosing party of any legitimate authority to order a trustee's sale."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 942-943 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)

A CourtListener index query restricted to this opinion's cluster returned zero results for the exact phrase "dated February 28, 2012", confirming the defect is in that publication's text and not in this extraction. Each quoted span here was checked to be free of such damage in both publications. No word, number or punctuation mark was changed. The second quote begins mid-sentence because the sentence straddles the break between pages 942 and 943 of the Official Reports; the page range in the cite reflects that.

THE LIMITS THE COURT PLACED ON ITS OWN RULING
Before reaching the facts, the Court described its ruling as a narrow one and stated three things it was not holding. It held only that a borrower who has suffered a nonjudicial foreclosure does not lack standing to sue for wrongful foreclosure on an allegedly void assignment merely because the borrower was in default and was not a party to the assignment. It did not hold or suggest that a borrower may preempt a threatened nonjudicial foreclosure by a suit questioning the foreclosing party's right to proceed. It did not hold that the plaintiff before it had alleged facts showing a void assignment or could prove them. And it did not address any of the substantive elements of the wrongful foreclosure tort or the factual showing needed to meet them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "Our ruling in this case is a narrow one. We hold only that a borrower who has suffered a nonjudicial foreclosure does not lack standing to sue for wrongful foreclosure based on an allegedly void assignment merely because he or she was in default on the loan and was not a party to the challenged assignment."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 924 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "We do not hold or suggest that a borrower may attempt to preempt a threatened nonjudicial foreclosure by a suit questioning the foreclosing party's right to proceed."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 924 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "Nor, finally, in rejecting defendants' arguments on standing do we address any of the substantive elements of the wrongful foreclosure tort or the factual showing necessary to meet those elements."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 924 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  Known gap: These are express self-limitations stated by the Court, and they are recorded here as negative results: the opinion resolves standing and nothing else. Because the Court declined to address the elements of the tort, this sheet cannot state what a wrongful foreclosure plaintiff must plead or prove beyond standing; a later Court of Appeal decision addressing the prejudice element is described in a separate clause and is not Supreme Court authority. All three quotes were verified against the courts.ca.gov slip PDF for S218973 (two extractors) and against the Official Reports text republished by CourtListener; all three sit on page 924 of the Official Reports by star pagination. Quotes were normalized only for benign extraction artifacts before comparison: non-breaking spaces, line-wrap hyphenation, ligatures, and the curly quotation marks and dashes that the two sources encode differently (the courts.ca.gov slip PDF renders opening and closing double quotation marks through a font mapping that extracts as U+2015 and U+2016, and em dashes extract as a double hyphen). No word, number or punctuation mark was changed.

WHO MAY DIRECT A TRUSTEE TO BEGIN AND COMPLETE A NONJUDICIAL FORECLOSURE
The reasoning rests on a proposition the Court treated as settled: although the trustee formally initiates a nonjudicial foreclosure by recording a notice of default and then a notice of sale, the trustee may take those steps only at the direction of the entity that currently holds the note and the beneficial interest under the deed of trust, or that entity's agent. The Court restated the point when it turned to the standing question, describing the entity holding the beneficial interest — the original lender, its assignee, or an agent of one of these — as the only one that may instruct the trustee to commence and complete a nonjudicial foreclosure. The Court also noted the general rules that a borrower can raise no objection to an assignment of the note, that a promissory note may be sold without notice to the borrower, and that the deed of trust follows the note even without a separate assignment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "the trustee may take these steps only at the direction of the person or entity that currently holds the note and the beneficial interest under the deed of trust-the original beneficiary or its assignee-or that entity's agent"
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 927 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "only the entity holding the beneficial interest under the deed of trust-the original lender, its assignee, or an agent of one of these-may instruct the trustee to commence and complete a nonjudicial foreclosure."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 935 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)

No word, number or punctuation mark was changed. In particular, the double hyphens inside the first quote correspond to em dashes in the Official Reports and to literal double hyphens in the slip PDF. This clause does not quote the opinion's sentence containing the phrase "well-established", because the slip PDF wraps that word across a line and de-hyphenation makes the two extractions disagree on it; the surrounding proposition is paraphrased instead. THE STATUTORY PROVISIONS THE COURT IDENTIFIED BUT DID NOT RELY ON
The plaintiff pointed to provisions added by the 2012 legislation known as the California Homeowner Bill of Rights. Civil Code section 2924, subdivision (a)(6) prohibits an entity from recording or causing the recording of a notice of default, or otherwise initiating the foreclosure process, unless it is the holder of the beneficial interest, the original or substituted trustee, or the designated agent of the holder of the beneficial interest. Civil Code section 2924.17, subdivision (b) requires a mortgage servicer, before recording or filing the documents listed in subdivision (a), to have reviewed competent and reliable evidence substantiating the borrower's default and the right to foreclose. The Court recorded that those provisions took effect only after the trustee's sale in that case and, having reached its conclusion without reference to the legislation, declined to decide whether they furnish additional support for it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "An entity shall not record or cause a notice of default to be recorded or otherwise initiate the foreclosure process unless it is the holder of the beneficial interest under the mortgage or deed of trust, the original trustee or the substituted trustee under the deed of trust, or the designated agent of the holder of the beneficial interest."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924(a)(6), Cal. Civ. Code § 2924, subd. (a)(6) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2924.)
  "Before recording or filing any of the documents described in subdivision (a), a mortgage servicer shall ensure that it has reviewed competent and reliable evidence to substantiate the borrower's default and the right to foreclose, including the borrower's loan status and loan information."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.17(b), Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.17, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2924.17.)
  "Having concluded without reference to this legislation that borrowers do have standing to challenge an assignment as void, we need not decide whether the new provisions provide additional support for that holding."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 942 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)

HOW THE COURT DEFINED VOID AND VOIDABLE
The Court reviewed the distinction on which its holding turns. A void contract, it said, is without legal effect; it binds no one and is a mere nullity, and neither action nor inaction of a party to it can validate it. A voidable transaction, by contrast, is one where one or more parties have the power, by a manifestation of election to do so, to avoid the legal relations created by the contract, or by ratification to extinguish the power of avoidance; it may be declared void but is not void in itself. The Court drew the consequence that matters for standing: unlike a voidable transaction, a void one cannot be ratified or validated by the parties to it even if they so desire.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "A void contract is without legal effect."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 929 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "is one where one or more parties have the power, by a manifestation of election to do so, to avoid the legal relations created by the contract, or by ratification of the contract to extinguish the power of avoidance."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 930 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "Unlike a voidable transaction, a void one cannot be ratified or validated by the parties to it even if they so desire."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 936 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)

The sentences attributed to Little v. CFS Service Corp. (1987) 188 Cal.App.3d 1354 and Colby v. Title Ins. and Trust Co. (1911) 160 Cal. 632 are likewise described only as the Yvanova Court reproduced them, and the Court of Appeal decision among them is not quoted independently. No word, number or punctuation mark was changed. The sentence stating that a voidable transaction is subject to ratification is paraphrased rather than quoted because it straddles a page break in the slip PDF, where the page number is extracted into the middle of the sentence.

WHY THE NONPARTY AND NO-PREJUDICE OBJECTIONS DID NOT DEFEAT STANDING
Two objections were pressed against borrower standing, and the Court answered both. The first was that a borrower who is neither a party to nor a third party beneficiary of an assignment cannot enforce its terms. The Court answered that a borrower alleging a void assignment is not attempting to enforce the instrument at all but urging that it is void ab initio, and is therefore asserting an interest of the borrower's own — an interest in limiting foreclosure on the property to those with legal authority to order a sale — rather than the interests of the parties to the assignment. The second objection was that a defaulting borrower suffers no prejudice, because the true beneficiary could equally have foreclosed. The Court answered that a foreclosed-upon borrower meets the general standard for standing by showing an invasion of legally protected interests, and that a borrower owes money not to the world at large but to a particular person or institution, only that person or institution being entitled to enforce the debt against the security.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]

  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 936 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "she is asserting her own interest in limiting foreclosure on her property to those with legal authority to order a foreclosure sale."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 937 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "A foreclosed-upon borrower clearly meets the general standard for standing to sue by showing an invasion of his or her legally protected interests"
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 937 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "The borrower owes money not to the world at large but to a particular person or institution, and only the person or institution entitled to payment may enforce the debt by foreclosing on the security."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 938 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)

All quotes were verified against the courts.ca.gov slip PDF for S218973 (pdfminer.six and pypdf) and against the Official Reports text republished by CourtListener. No word, number or punctuation mark was changed. What counts as prejudice for purposes of the tort itself, as opposed to standing, was expressly left open; see the following clause.

TENDER AND PREJUDICE AS ELEMENTS: EXPRESSLY LEFT UNDECIDED
The Court separated two senses of prejudice. In the body of the opinion it said it was concerned only with prejudice in the sense of an injury sufficiently concrete and personal to provide standing, and not with prejudice as a possible element of the wrongful foreclosure tort. In a footnote it noted that it has been held that a plaintiff seeking to set aside a foreclosure sale must also show prejudice and a tender of the amount of the secured indebtedness, or an excuse of tender, and that tender has been excused where the foreclosure deed is alleged to be facially void. The Court then expressly declined to say whether the plaintiff before it had to allege tender, and declined to address prejudice as an element of the tort. Whether tender or its excuse would be required of anyone with respect to 123 Main St., Woodland Hills, CA 91367 is therefore not answered by this decision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "In deciding the limited question on review, we are concerned only with prejudice in the sense of an injury sufficiently concrete and personal to provide standing, not with prejudice as a possible element of the wrongful foreclosure tort."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 937 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "Our review being limited to the standing question, we express no opinion as to whether plaintiff Yvanova must allege tender to state a cause of action for wrongful foreclosure under the circumstances of this case."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, fn. 4 (2016) (no page pin cite; see gap) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  "As to prejudice, we do not address it as an element of wrongful foreclosure."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, fn. 4 (2016) (no page pin cite; see gap) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)

The slip PDF is not star-paginated at all. Rather than infer a page, this sheet cites the footnote by number, as the opinion itself does when it refers back to it. SUITS BROUGHT BEFORE A SALE: OUTSIDE THE SCOPE OF THE DECISION
The Court of Appeal decision the Supreme Court disapproved, Jenkins v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 497, had rested on two grounds. One was that California law does not permit a preemptive judicial action to challenge the authority of a foreclosing beneficiary or its agent to initiate and pursue foreclosure. The Supreme Court stated that this aspect of Jenkins was not within the scope of its review, which was limited to a borrower's standing to challenge an assignment in an action seeking remedies for wrongful foreclosure, and that the concrete question before it concerned a trustee's sale that had already taken place. It expressly did not address whether, or under what circumstances, a borrower may bring an action for injunctive or declaratory relief to prevent a foreclosure sale from going forward.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "whether, or under what circumstances, a borrower may bring an action for injunctive or declaratory relief to prevent a foreclosure sale from going forward."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 934 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  Known gap: The quote is shortened at its start, and deliberately so. The full sentence in the opinion begins "We do not address the distinct question of whether...", but the Official Reports text republished by CourtListener prints "dishnct" for "distinct" — scan damage in that publication, which the courts.ca.gov slip PDF for S218973 does not share. Rather than silently correct the word or quote a span that is not verbatim in both publications, the quote begins after it and the defect is disclosed here. The remainder of the quoted span is verbatim in the slip PDF (both extractors) and in the CourtListener text. Quotes were normalized only for benign extraction artifacts before comparison: non-breaking spaces, line-wrap hyphenation, ligatures, and the curly quotation marks and dashes that the two sources encode differently (the courts.ca.gov slip PDF renders opening and closing double quotation marks through a font mapping that extracts as U+2015 and U+2016, and em dashes extract as a double hyphen). No word, number or punctuation mark was changed. Jenkins is a Court of Appeal decision and is described here only as the Supreme Court characterized it; this sheet does not quote it independently.

POST-CLOSING-DATE TRANSFERS INTO A SECURITIZED TRUST: EXPRESSLY NOT DECIDED
Glaski v. Bank of America (2013) 218 Cal.App.4th 1079 had held both that a borrower may challenge an assignment as void and, separately, that allegations of a transfer into a securitized investment trust after the trust's closing date sufficed to plead a void assignment. The Supreme Court took up only the first holding. It stated that on granting review it had limited the question to borrower standing, that it did not include the question whether a post-closing date transfer into a New York securitized trust is void or merely voidable, and that although the parties' briefs addressed the point it expressed no opinion on it. It repeated that reservation when distinguishing the Second Circuit's contrary view of New York law in Rajamin v. Deutsche Bank Nat. Trust Co. (2d Cir. 2014) 757 F.3d 79.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "We did not include in our order the question of whether a postclosing date transfer into a New York securitized trust is void or merely voidable, and though the parties' briefs address it, we express no opinion on the question here."
  — Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp., 62 Cal.4th 919, 931 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3178579/yvanova-v-new-century-mortgage-corp/)
  Known gap: This clause records an express reservation, not a holding. The consequence is that Yvanova does not decide whether the kind of defect most often alleged in securitization cases renders an assignment void or merely voidable; a later published Court of Appeal decision answering that question under New York law is described in a separate clause of this sheet and is not Supreme Court authority. The quoted sentence contains the word "postclosing" without a hyphen, which is how both publications print it — this is not a de-hyphenation artifact; the slip PDF sets the word on a single line. The quote was verified against the courts.ca.gov slip PDF for S218973 (pdfminer.six and pypdf) and against the Official Reports text republished by CourtListener, and the pin cite was read off star pagination. Quotes were normalized only for benign extraction artifacts before comparison: non-breaking spaces, line-wrap hyphenation, ligatures, and the curly quotation marks and dashes that the two sources encode differently (the courts.ca.gov slip PDF renders opening and closing double quotation marks through a font mapping that extracts as U+2015 and U+2016, and em dashes extract as a double hyphen). No word, number or punctuation mark was changed.

WHICH COURT OF APPEAL DECISIONS WERE APPROVED AND WHICH WERE DISAPPROVED
The Court resolved a split among Court of Appeal decisions. It concluded that Glaski was correct to hold that a wrongful foreclosure plaintiff has standing to claim that the foreclosing entity's purported authority to order a trustee's sale rested on a void assignment of the note and deed of trust, and that Jenkins had spoken too broadly in holding that a borrower lacks standing to challenge an assignment to which the borrower was neither a party nor a third party beneficiary. In a footnote the Court disapproved four decisions — Jenkins, Siliga v. Mortgage Electronic Registration Systems, Inc. (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 75, Fontenot v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. (2011) 198 Cal.App.4th 256, and Herrera v. Federal National Mortgage Assn. (2012) 205 Cal.App.4th 1495 — to the extent stated in the quoted language. The Court added that Jenkins's rule may still hold as to claimed defects that would make an assignment merely voidable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "we conclude Glaski, supra, 218 Cal.App.4th 1079, was correct to hold a wrongful foreclosure plaintiff has standing to claim the foreclosing entity's purported authority to order a trustee's sale was based on a void assignment of the note and deed of trust."

A COURT OF APPEAL ANSWER TO THE PREJUDICE QUESTION YVANOVA LEFT OPEN

expectedJSON.body: The Court reviewed the distinction on which its holding turns. A void contract, it said, is without legal effect; it binds no one and is a mere nullity, and neither action nor inaction of a party to it can validate it. A voidable transaction, by contrast, is one where one or more parties have the power, by a manifestation of election to do so, to avoid the legal relations created by the contract, or by ratification to extinguish the power of avoidance; it may be declared void but is not void in itself. The Court drew the consequence that matters for standing: unlike a voidable transaction, a void one cannot be ratified or validated by the parties to it even if they so desire.

The first was that a borrower who is neither a party to nor a third party beneficiary of an assignment cannot enforce its terms. The Court answered that a borrower alleging a void assignment is not attempting to enforce the instrument at all but urging that it is void ab initio, and is therefore asserting an interest of the borrower's own — an interest in limiting foreclosure on the property to those with legal authority to order a sale — rather than the interests of the parties to the assignment. The Court answered that a foreclosed-upon borrower meets the general standard for standing by showing an invasion of legally protected interests, and that a borrower owes money not to the world at large but to a particular person or institution, only that person or institution being entitled to enforce the debt against the security.

It stated that on granting review it had limited the question to borrower standing, that it did not include the question whether a post-closing date transfer into a New York securitized trust is void or merely voidable, and that although the parties' briefs addressed the point it expressed no opinion on it. It repeated that reservation when distinguishing the Second Circuit's contrary view of New York law in Rajamin v. Deutsche Bank Nat. Trust Co. (2d Cir. 2014) 757 F.3d 79.

expectedJSON.body: The Court resolved a split among Court of Appeal decisions. It concluded that Glaski was correct to hold that a wrongful foreclosure plaintiff has standing to claim that the foreclosing entity's purported authority to order a trustee's sale rested on a void assignment of the note and deed of trust, and that Jenkins had spoken too broadly in holding that a borrower lacks standing to challenge an assignment to which the borrower was neither a party nor a third party beneficiary. In a footnote the Court disapproved four decisions — Jenkins, Siliga v. Mortgage Electronic Registration Systems, Inc. (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 75, Fontenot v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. (2011) 198 Cal.App.4th 256, and Herrera v. Federal National Mortgage Assn. (2012) 205 Cal.App.4th 1495 — to the extent stated in the quoted language. The Court added that Jenkins's rule may still hold as to claimed defects that would make an assignment merely voidable.

expectedJSON.body: Three months after Yvanova, the Court of Appeal in Sciarratta v. U.S. Bank National Assn. (2016) 247 Cal.App.4th 552 took up the prejudice question the Supreme Court had reserved. The court framed the issue as whether allegations of foreclosure by one with no right to do so establish by themselves the prejudice or harm needed to state a wrongful foreclosure cause of action, or whether the plaintiff must additionally allege that the wrongful foreclosure interfered with the ability to pay the debt or produced a foreclosure that would not otherwise have occurred. It concluded that such allegations suffice on their own, reasoning that a homeowner is harmed by losing the home to an entity with no legal right to take it, and reversed a judgment of dismissal entered after a demurrer was sustained without leave to amend.
